All About Measles: A Collaborative Case Study

Authors: Kirsten Casey, Alaina Durant, Taeyeon Kim, and Celia Ligorski

Class: Principles of Epidemiology

Semester: Autumn 2026

Overview

Measles, sometimes called rubeola, is one of the most contagious known viruses which is spread via respiratory droplets when an infected person breathes, coughs, or sneezes. The virus can remain airborne and active outside the body for up to two hours, and an infected person is contagious for four days before any symptoms appear, so they may spread the virus before they are aware of any illness. Measles most commonly affects children, but it can be spread to anyone who is not immune; an estimated 90% of non-immune people who come in contact with an infected person will contract the disease. Vaccination is the best way to protect oneself and others from measles infection.

In the United States, measles was declared eliminated in 2000, but it remains endemic in Africa, Southeast Asia, the Eastern Mediterranean, and the Western Pacific regions as defined by the World Health Organization (WHO). Measles outbreaks in the United States can still occur when people (often Americans) travel into the country, particularly if they come in contact with under- or unvaccinated communities. In recent years, outbreaks in the United States have become more common, driven predominantly by vaccine hesitancy.

Symptoms & Diagnosis

• Timeline
• Symptoms
• Diagnosis

Timeline

The timeline. After exposure, there is an incubation period of about 10–14 days (range 7–21) before the first symptoms appear (Stoneman, JAMA, 2025).

Symptoms

The prodrome (“the 3 Cs”). Illness begins with a 2–4 day period of high fever plus cough, coryza (runny nose), and conjunctivitis (red, watery eyes) — the classic “three Cs.” Fever can climb above 40 °C (104 °F). The conjunctivitis is often severe, with tearing and sensitivity to light (Naureckas Li et al., Pediatrics, 2025; Do & Mulholland, New England Journal of Medicine, 2025).

Koplik spots. During the prodrome, tiny white or bluish-white spots on a red background may appear inside the cheeks (buccal mucosa). These Koplik spots are pathognomonic — meaning they are unique to measles — but they are easy to miss because they last only 1–3 days and most people do not seek care that early (Rota et al., Nature Reviews Disease Primers, 2016; Naureckas Li et al., Pediatrics, 2025).

The rash. About 2–4 days after the fever starts (roughly 14 days after exposure), the characteristic red, blotchy, maculopapular rash appears. It starts at the hairline and behind the ears, then spreads downward to the face, trunk, arms, and legs. It typically begins bright red and blanching, then turns coppery-brown, and often peels (desquamates) as it fades in the same order it appeared. The rash usually lasts about a week; the cough can linger longer than 10 days (Naureckas Li et al., Pediatrics, 2025; Goodson & Filardo, CDC Yellow Book, 2025).

Diagnosis

When to suspect measles. Measles should be considered in anyone with fever plus a rash, especially if they are unvaccinated, have recently traveled internationally or to a U.S. area with a known outbreak, or had a known exposure within the past 21 days (Stoneman, JAMA, 2025).

How it is diagnosed. Clinical suspicion must be confirmed by laboratory testing:

  • RT-PCR (reverse transcriptase-polymerase chain reaction) from a throat or nasopharyngeal swab is the preferred test; adding a urine sample increases sensitivity. Viral RNA is detectable for about 3 days after rash onset (sensitivity ~94%, specificity ~99%) (Stoneman, JAMA, 2025; Naureckas Li et al., Pediatrics, 2025).
  • Serum measles-specific IgM antibody is typically detectable 3–30 days after rash onset. (Measles-specific IgG appears later and indicates immunity from past infection or vaccination) (Stoneman, JAMA, 2025).

A key point: any suspected case should prompt an immediate call to the local health department and hospital infection prevention team for guidance on testing and isolation, because there is no rapid point-of-care test — samples must be sent to a lab (Stoneman, JAMA, 2025).

Transmission & Spread

• Transmission
• Spread
• Surveillance

Transmission

The basic reproductive number, R0, is often used as a measure of transmissibility, representing the expected number of individuals to whom an infected person will spread a given disease assuming no immunity.

R0 for measles and common viruses:

  • Human rhinovirus (common cold): R0 ~ 1.2-2.6
  • Seasonal flu: R0 ~ 2-3
  • COVID-19: R0 ~ 3.3
  • Measles: R0 ~ 12-18
Spread

Transmission of measles can be interrupted and the effective R0 can be reduced if enough people in a population are immune; because measles is so contagious, 95% of people in a community must be fully vaccinated to control further spread. The WHO estimates that worldwide in 2025, approximately 77% of children received both recommended doses of the MMR vaccine with 84% receiving only the first dose. There are ongoing immunization partnerships between the WHO and local organizations in every region of the world working towards the goal of measles elimination.

Surveillance

In the United States, measles is a notifiable disease, meaning confirmed or suspected cases should be reported to the local health department as soon as possible to support public health investigations. Investigative responses to measles outbreaks typically involve vaccination campaigns in addition to case investigation, contact tracing, and isolation of infected individuals. Many factors influence the effectiveness of measles surveillance and elimination efforts in the United States; the COVID-19 pandemic in particular interrupted planned vaccination and surveillance campaigns and exacerbated vaccine hesitancy and refusal. Socioeconomic factors also play a significant role in the ability of public health officials to respond to outbreaks; crowded or uncertain living conditions, low educational attainment, and lack of access to sufficient healthcare are all correlated with increased risk of measles infection and worse outcomes. As a result, the United States and other regions around the world are experiencing more frequent outbreaks and caseloads in recent years.

Treatment & Prevention

• Treatment
• Prevention
• After an Exposure
• During an Active Outbreak

Treatment

There is no specific antiviral treatment for measles. Care is supportive. It focuses on managing fever, keeping the patient hydrated, watching for complications and treating them, and preventing the spread to other people. For young children, two doses of vitamin A are also recommended because they lower the risk of death from measles (Bester, 2016).

Prevention

The best prevention is the MMR vaccine. One dose is 95% effective at preventing measles and 92% effective at preventing spread to household contacts. When the first dose is given at 12 months or older, 95% of children develop immunity. With a second dose, more than 99% develop immunity (Bester, 2016). In the United States, the CDC recommends the first dose at 12 to 15 months of age and the second dose at 4 to 6 years. Doses given before 12 months do not count as valid doses. To stop measles from spreading in a community, 93% to 95% of the population needs to be immune, so two-dose vaccination coverage needs to stay at that level. Common side effects of the vaccine, such as fever or a mild rash, are mild and go away on their own. Serious side effects are very rare (Bester, 2016).

After an Exposure

If a person who is not immune is exposed to measles, the MMR vaccine can still be given within 72 hours of exposure. Immune globulin can be given within 6 days of exposure. In the 2022 central Ohio outbreak, 59 exposed contacts received one of these, and none of the 51 who received immune globulin developed measles (Tiller et al., 2023).

During an Active Outbreak
  • For families: Check your MMR status now. A dose given within 72 hours of a known exposure can still prevent illness.
  • For the public: Call ahead before walking into a clinic or ED with suspected measles, don’t just show up.
  • For providers: Think measles in any child with fever and rash, and report it the same day you suspect it. Patients are contagious before the rash ever appears.

Provider Information

• Recognize, Isolate, Report
• Communication Tips
• Vaccine Myths vs. Facts

Recognize, Isolate, Report
  • Think of measles early. Suspect measles in any patient, especially in those patients w/ unknown or incomplete vaccination status who presents with fever ≥38.3°C (101°F) plus cough, coryza, or conjunctivitis, and a generalized maculopapular rash. Suspicion should rise further with recent travel to an outbreak area, a known exposure, or residence in a community with under-vaccinated pockets, even if the broader region’s coverage looks adequate on paper. Do not wait for the rash or koplik spots.
  • Isolate immediately. Isolate on suspicion, not on confirmation. Place the suspected patient in airborne isolation and mask the patient. The virus can linger in the air for up to 2 hours, a suspected case in a busy waiting room can expose MANY many vulnerable people. Patients are shedding virus before they, or you, know they’re infected. Ask families who suspect measles to call ahead rather than walking into a crowded ED or clinic.
  • Report and Coordinate. Notify the local or state health department and infection prevention team as soon as measles is suspected - BEFORE THE TEST RETURNS. Measles is a nationally notifiable disease. A day or two of delay can close the window for effective contact tracing and post-exposure prophylaxis. Offer post-exposure prophylaxis to identified contacts: MMR vaccine within 72 hours of exposure, or immune globulin within 6 days, prioritizing infants, pregnant patients, and immunocompromised contacts who cannot receive the live vaccine.
  • Confirm with Testing. Test with nasopharyngeal/throat PCR (highly sensitive, and allows genotyping to link cases during an outbreak) and/or serum IgM.
  • Protect your waiting room. Screen for fever, rash, travel, and vaccine status before a patient enters common space, and give patients/families a way to call ahead if they suspect measles. In the 2022–2023 central Ohio outbreak, 38% of exposures occurred inside healthcare facilities — more than in households or child care settings — because the first cases weren’t recognized before they reached a waiting room (Tiller et al., 2023).
As a Provider, how should I communicate with my patients?
  • Lead with curiosity and listening, not correction or lecturing.
    • Ask open, non judgmental questions to understand each families concerns, what they’ve read or heard, and where, before responding. Understanding the real concern lets you address it directly.
    • Ask about the reasons behind the hesitancy, not just the myths. Cultural, religious, or access barriers call for a different conversation than misinformation does — and pointing families toward sources they already trust works better than only offering your own.
  • Skip the scare tactics. Rather make the risk concrete and personal.
    • Explain that the measles is not a mild illness- it can cause pneumonia, brain inflammation and death and it can suppress the immune system for years. (Stoneman, JAMA, 2025; Do & Mulholland, New England Journal of Medicine, 2025).
    • Reviews of vaccine-communication strategies have found that graphic images, dramatic anecdotes, and dire warnings can backfire and entrench resistance rather than change minds. Speaking with total certainty can have the same effect (Whitehead et al., 2023).
  • “Pre-bunk” when you can.
    • Giving families accurate information before they encounter misinformation is more effective than trying to correct it afterward (Whitehead et al., 2023).
  • Address the autism claim clearly and calmly.
    • The claim that the MMR vaccine causes autism originate in 1998 paper, an uncontrolled, single, small (12-child) study that was later retracted for fraude and its author lost his medical license. Numerous large, multicenter studies have since been completed that have found NO LINK between MMR and Autism. A Cochrane review of the much larger body of research published since found no association.
  • Be honest about real side effects.
    • They exist — typically mild and self-limited fever, rash, or joint pain — and serious reactions are rare. Minimizing legitimate safety questions undermines trust more than it reassures.
  • Acknowledge the choice to vaccinate, every time.
    • A brief “thank you for protecting your community” costs nothing and can ease the discomfort many families feel even bringing the topic up.
    • Frame vaccination as protecting the whole community. Vaccination projects not only the child but infants, too young to be vaccinated and immunocompromised neighbors who depend on herd immunity (95% vaccination).
  • Build the relationship before the crisis.
    • Trust formed over routine visits is what a family draws on when they’re deciding whether to believe you in the middle of an outbreak.
Myths vs. Facts: The MMR Vaccine

Myth 1: “The MMR vaccine causes autism.”
Fact: It does not. This claim came from a single 1998 paper that was retracted for fraud, and its author lost his medical license. Since then, studies of millions of children have found no link. A nationwide study of 657,461 children found no increased autism risk in vaccinated children (hazard ratio 0.93), and a Cochrane review of the combined evidence reached the same conclusion (Hviid et al., Annals of Internal Medicine, 2019; Di Pietrantonj et al., Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 2021).

Myth 2: “Mercury (thimerosal) in the MMR shot is dangerous.”
Fact: The MMR vaccine has never contained thimerosal or any mercury preservative. Separately, the type of mercury once used in a few other vaccines (ethylmercury) is cleared by the body quickly and is not the harmful kind (methylmercury). Expert reviews found no link between thimerosal and autism (Larson et al., New England Journal of Medicine, 2022; AAP Red Book, 2024–2027).

Myth 3: “Aluminum or ‘fetal cells’ in vaccines are harmful.”
Fact: The MMR vaccine does not contain aluminum. Vaccines do not contain cells or DNA from aborted fetuses. Where aluminum is used as an adjuvant in other vaccines, the amount is tiny, regulated, and similar to what infants take in through breast milk or formula (AAP Red Book, 2024–2027; O’Leary et al., Pediatrics/AAP, 2024).

Myth 4: “It’s safer to space out shots or give them one at a time.”
Fact: There is no benefit to splitting the combination MMR into separate shots, and doing so only prolongs the time a child is unprotected. A child’s immune system easily handles the antigens in routine vaccines alongside the countless germs it meets every day (CDC MMR Vaccine Safety, 2024; AAP Red Book, 2024–2027).

Myth 5: “Natural infection gives better immunity than the vaccine.”
Fact: “Natural” measles immunity comes at a steep price: pneumonia, brain inflammation, and death are all possible, and measles can wipe out the immune system’s memory for years (“immune amnesia”), leaving a child vulnerable to other infections. Even complications like low-platelet bleeding (ITP) are more common after natural infection than after the vaccine (Do & Mulholland, New England Journal of Medicine, 2025; Di Pietrantonj et al., Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 2021).

Myth 6: “The vaccine is more dangerous than the disease.”
Fact: Serious reactions to MMR are very rare. Mild effects (sore arm, brief fever, mild rash) are common; febrile seizures (MMRV, not MMR) occur in roughly 1 in 3,000–4,000 doses and have no lasting effects. By contrast, measles itself kills 1–3 of every 1,000 people infected and causes complications in up to about 30% of cases (ACIP/McLean et al., 2013; Stoneman, JAMA, 2025; Do & Mulholland, New England Journal of Medicine, 2025).

Myth 7: “Measles is just a harmless childhood rash.”
Fact: Measles can be severe. Complications include ear infections and hearing loss, pneumonia (the leading cause of measles death), encephalitis (about 1 per 1,000–2,000 cases), and the rare, always-fatal (fatal in 100% of patients) brain disease SSPE years later. Infants, pregnant people, and immunocompromised people are at highest risk (Stoneman, JAMA, 2025; Do & Mulholland, New England Journal of Medicine, 2025).

The bottom line: Two doses of MMR are about 97% effective and have a decades-long safety record. Vaccination protects your child and the people around them who can’t be vaccinated — newborns and those with weakened immune systems (Gastañaduy et al., Journal of Infectious Diseases, 2021; Stoneman, JAMA, 2025).
